SECTION 010:00–3:14

The system and the plan

Solve Ax = b by elimination, then back substitution.

Lecture 1 showed what a solution means geometrically. Lecture 2 develops a systematic way to find it. Strang’s example is

x + 2y + z = 2
3x + 8y + z = 12
4y + z = 2.

The matrix notation is

[121381041][xyz]=[2122]

Elimination replaces equations by combinations that remove unknowns one at a time. The aim is an upper triangular system: first remove x from the lower equations, then remove y from the last equation.

Once that triangular system is available, back substitution solves the last equation first and works upward. The second part of the lecture writes the elimination steps themselves as matrix multiplications.

SECTION 023:14–6:54

Use the first pivot to remove x

The multiplier is the entry to eliminate divided by the pivot.

The first pivot is the 1 in the top-left corner of A. The first row is the pivot row and stays unchanged. To remove the 3 below that pivot, subtract three copies of row 1 from row 2:

R₂ ← R₂ − 3R₁.

The multiplier is 3/1 = 3. Work through the entire row, not just its first entry:

3 − 3·1 = 0
8 − 3·2 = 2
1 − 3·1 = −2.

After this operation, the coefficient matrix is

[12102−2041]

The position (3, 1), meaning row 3 and column 1, is already zero. Its multiplier is therefore zero, and no change to row 3 is needed. The first column is now cleared below the pivot.

The row-operation convention

Strang subtracts the multiplier times the pivot row. This convention explains the negative signs in the elimination matrices introduced later.

SECTION 036:54–10:34

Use the second pivot to reach U

A second elimination step reveals the third pivot.

The next pivot is the 2 in the updated second row. The entry beneath it is 4, so the next multiplier is 4/2 = 2. Use the updated row 2:

R₃ ← R₃ − 2R₂.

The new last row is (0, 4, 1) − 2(0, 2, −2) = (0, 0, 5). In particular, the last entry is 1 − 2(−2) = 5. Thus elimination transforms A into

U=[12102−2005]

U is upper triangular: every entry below its diagonal is zero. Its pivots are 1, 2, and 5, all nonzero. This example therefore completes elimination without any row exchanges.

Strang briefly anticipates determinants: for this example, which required no row exchanges, the determinant is the product of the pivots, 1·2·5 = 10.

Board correction retained in context. During the lecture Strang briefly copies −2 as −1 and then corrects it. The study equations and redraw use the corrected −2; the transcript retains the original spoken sequence.

SECTION 0410:34–14:34

When a pivot position contains zero

Distinguish a repairable row ordering from genuine singularity.

A pivot used for elimination must be nonzero. A zero in the next pivot position does not automatically mean the whole system is hopeless: a nonzero entry lower in that column may be brought up by exchanging rows.

A temporary difficulty

Suppose the original 8 in row 2 were 6. Subtracting three copies of row 1 would then produce (0, 0, −2). There would be zero in the second pivot position, but the next row would still be (0, 4, 1). Exchange rows 2 and 3 and use the 4 as the next pivot.

A singular case

Instead, restore the original 8 and change the original bottom-right entry from 1 to −4. The last row would begin as (0, 4, −4). The final elimination step would give

(0, 4, −4) − 2(0, 2, −2) = (0, 0, 0).

No third pivot remains, and there is no lower row available for an exchange. This altered square matrix is singular, or not invertible.

The important distinction is between a zero that a row exchange can repair and a genuine shortage of pivots. A singular matrix does not provide a unique solution for every right-hand side.

SECTION 0514:34–19:08

Carry b along, then substitute backward

The same row operations turn b into c.

So far we have focused on the coefficient matrix. To solve the equations, the right-hand side must undergo exactly the same row operations. Appending b as an extra column gives the augmented matrix, written [A | b].

Initially b = (2, 12, 2)T. The first operation leaves the first and third entries fixed and changes the second to 12 − 3·2 = 6. The second operation changes the third to 2 − 2·6 = −10:

[2122]→[262]→[26−10]

Call the final right-hand side c. The original system Ax = b has become Ux = c:

x + 2y + z = 2
2y − 2z = 6
5z = −10.

Start at the bottom. The last equation gives z = −2. Substitute that into the second: 2y + 4 = 6, so y = 1. Finally substitute both values into the first: x + 2 − 2 = 2, so x = 2.

x = 2,   y = 1,   z = −2.

The order is reversed because the system is triangular. Checking the original three equations gives 2, 12, and 2 on their left-hand sides, exactly the original b.

SECTION 0619:08–24:33

Multiplication combines columns or rows

The side of multiplication determines which vectors are combined.

Strang now shifts from writing matrix entries to writing the operations as matrices. He first recalls the column interpretation from Lecture 1.

If a matrix A is multiplied on the right by the column (3, 4, 5)T, the result is a column vector: three times column 1 plus four times column 2 plus five times column 3.

The parallel row interpretation is equally important. Multiply A on the left by the row (1, 2, 7). The result is a row vector: one times row 1 plus two times row 2 plus seven times row 3.

RIGHT

A times a column

A linear combination of the columns of A.

LEFT

A row times A

A linear combination of the rows of A.

ELIMINATION

Combine rows

Place the operation matrix on the left.

This is the reason an elimination matrix multiplies A from the left: elimination changes rows by taking combinations of rows.

SECTION 0724:33–32:21

Build the elimination matrices

Start with the identity and insert the negative multiplier.

What matrix subtracts three times row 1 from row 2 while leaving the other rows unchanged? Its first row must be (1, 0, 0), so it selects row 1. Its third row must be (0, 0, 1), so it selects row 3. Its second row is (−3, 1, 0), giving −3 times row 1 plus row 2.

E21=[100−310001]

This differs from the identity matrix only in position (2, 1), where −3 has been inserted. The subscript records the position being cleared. Multiplying on the left gives the first elimination step:

E21A=[12102−2041]

For the second step, keep rows 1 and 2 and replace row 3 by row 3 minus two copies of row 2. The required matrix is

E32=[1000100−21]

Again, the negative multiplier sits in the position being cleared, (3, 2). Applying E₃₂ to the updated matrix gives U.

Check one product entry

The (2, 3) entry of E₂₁A is the dot product of row 2 of E₂₁ and column 3 of A: (−3)·1 + 1·1 + 0·1 = −2. This agrees with the row-operation calculation.

SECTION 0832:21–36:34

Combine the steps without changing their order

Associativity moves the parentheses; it does not reverse the factors.

We start with A, apply E₂₁, and then apply E₃₂. The whole elimination process is

E₃₂(E₂₁A) = U.

The associative law allows the parentheses to move:

E₃₂(E₂₁A) = (E₃₂E₂₁)A = U.

The factors remain in the same order. We may either do two successive operations on A or first multiply the elimination matrices to obtain one matrix that does the whole job.

Working out the product of the matrices already on the board gives

E32E21=[100−3106−21]

The 6 in the lower-left corner records the interaction between the two operations. The product acts on A to give U, and on b to give c.

Worked expansion. Strang gives the associative expression and discusses combining the steps. The numerical product shown here is an editorial expansion of those same matrices.

Keep the order: the factor immediately next to A acts first. Moving parentheses is permitted; swapping matrix factors generally is not.

SECTION 0936:34–42:06

Exchange rows or columns with P

Left multiplication changes rows; right multiplication changes columns.

A row exchange is also a matrix operation. To exchange two rows, perform that exchange on the identity matrix. In two dimensions, the resulting permutation matrix is

P=[0110]

For a general matrix A with first row (a, b) and second row (c, d), PA has first row (c, d) and second row (a, b). The permutation matrix is on the left because it combines rows.

To exchange the columns instead, put P on the right. Then AP has first row (b, a) and second row (d, c). Its first column selects the old second column; its second selects the old first.

Which side?

Row operations multiply on the left. Column operations multiply on the right.

This also shows why matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: PA and AP perform different operations and usually give different results. The associative law remains valid even though the commutative law fails.

SECTION 1042:06–47:23

Undo an elimination step with an inverse

Add back the multiple that was subtracted.

In the final part of the lecture, Strang looks ahead to inverses. Rather than only asking how to go from A to U, ask how to undo an elimination step.

E₂₁ subtracted three times row 1 from row 2. Its inverse must add those three copies back. Rows 1 and 3 still stay fixed:

E21−1=[100310001]

For example, E₂₁ changed b = (2, 12, 2)T into (2, 6, 2)T. The inverse changes the second entry back to 3·2 + 6 = 12.

Applying an operation and then undoing it leaves everything unchanged. In matrix notation, that means

E₂₁⁻¹E₂₁ = I.

The cancellation can be checked in the second row of the product: three times the first row of E₂₁ plus its second row gives (0, 1, 0), the second row of the identity.

The lecture stops after this first example of an inverse. The next lecture develops matrix multiplication and inverse matrices further.
